description: The conformance corpus for standards/038-feature-flags.md. Six parts. 'declarations' is judged by flag-declaration.schema.json alone; 'contexts' by evaluation-context.schema.json alone; 'evaluated_sets' by evaluated-set.schema.json alone — each case is accepted or rejected and a rejection names the rule. 'evaluation' is judged by running an evaluation boundary: given the fixture declarations, a provider state and a context, the call must return exactly the stated value, reason and error code and raise exactly the stated findings (FF1, FF2, FF4, FF6). 'gating' is judged by serving a request behind an entitlement flag and a permission check together (FF5). 'experiments' is judged by evaluating a split flag repeatedly and counting distinct variants per subject and exposures recorded (FF10). 'expiry' is judged by comparing a declaration to a date and listing the findings the sweep raises (FF3, FF11). Five cases are detectors: 'provider-unavailable-returns-the-declared-default' fails an implementation that fails open on provider error; 'an-undeclared-flag-is-a-finding' fails an implementation that asks the provider before the declaration; 'entitled-and-denied-is-refused' fails an implementation that treats a flag as authorization; 'a-review-date-beyond-the-year-exceeds-the-horizon' fails a sweep with no forward ceiling on review_by; 'a-long-lived-flag-reviewed-recently-is-admitted' fails a sweep bounding review_by from created rather than from the reading date.

contexts.why: FF6 in full: the targeting key is the tenant's public id, the id vocabulary is 040 OC2's, the environment is spelled as WC2 spells it, and the attributes are a plan tier and a region.
FF6: a global flag needs no targeting key; the environment is the one required key, in place of environment detection in code.
FF6: the provider stores what it receives, and an email address is personal data in a third system. A rule that targets a person targets a public id.
FF6: the denylist is a substring match on the key, so the common renamings do not pass it.
FF6: a string value containing @ is an email address in almost every case, whatever the key is called.
FF6: attributes are flat scalars. A nested object is how a whole record travels to the provider.
IP1 through FF6: the targeting key is a public id; an integer is an internal key that never leaves the service, and here it would leave it to a provider.
FF6: the context is closed to the vocabulary; a person's name is not in it and cannot be added by putting it at the top level instead of under attributes.
FF6: the environment is the one key every evaluation carries, because it is the one every rule may need and the one code may not detect for itself (030 SC3).
FF6 and 050 HA8: attribute keys are snake_case on the wire, like every other field name that leaves the service.

evaluated_sets.why: FF7: flag name to scalar value, and the instant the server evaluated it.
FF2 through FF7: the browser's names are the declaration's names, so the client and the server are talking about the same flag.
FF7: object-typed flags are not served to the client; a document of rules or settings in the browser is configuration the client cannot be trusted to evaluate.
IP4 through FF7: emitted instants are UTC with a Z suffix.

evaluation.why: FF1: the ordinary path. The provider has a rule for this tenant; the typed call returns its value with the specification's reason.
FF1: another tenant meets no rule and receives the provider's fallback, reason STATIC — the provider answered, so this is not the declared default.

FF2 and FF4: declared in the repository, not yet configured at the provider — the state of every flag between its first commit and its first dashboard entry. The provider reports FLAG_NOT_FOUND; the application receives the declared default and logs the first occurrence. No finding: the declaration exists.

FF4, the detector. The provider is down; the call returns the declared default, false, with PROVIDER_NOT_READY. An implementation that fails open — returns true on provider error, because it was written while the feature was being turned on — returns true here and passes every case in which the provider is up.

FF2, the detector. The provider holds a flag no declaration names — created in a dashboard, invisible in the repository. The boundary returns the call's default with FLAG_NOT_FOUND, raises undeclared_flag, and never asks the provider. An implementation that asks the provider first returns the provider's true here and passes every case whose flag is declared.
FF1 and FF4: the provider answers with a string for a boolean flag. Evaluation is typed; the value is refused with TYPE_MISMATCH and the declared default is returned.

FF2 and FF6: the declaration says scope tenant and the context carries no tenant. The provider is not asked; the declared default returns with TARGETING_KEY_MISSING. A missing context denies, as 025 SD6 has it for isolation.

FF4: the call site passed true where the declaration says false. The provider answered, so the value is the provider's; the disagreement is a finding for the diff, because on the day the provider is down the two defaults would give two different answers.
FF3 and FF9: a kill switch is global, needs no targeting key, and an operator has set it at the provider. true here is the intervention, per FF4's naming rule.
FF4 for a non-boolean: the declared default is the variant the code shipped with, and it is what an outage returns.

gating.why: FF5: the entitlement says the capability is offered to this tenant and the permission says this subject may use it. Both yes; served.

FF5, the detector. The flag is on and the permission check denies; the request is refused. An implementation that serves because the flag was on has made a flag dashboard the access-control system, and it passes the other three cases.
FF5: the subject may use a capability the tenant does not have. The route answers as if the code were not deployed — 404 per 050 HA3 — so a dark capability is dark to enumeration.
FF5: the flag is evaluated first because it decides whether the route exists; a route that does not exist has no permission to deny.

experiments.why: FF10: assignment is a pure function of the flag name and the targeting key, so three evaluations for one subject produce one variant and one exposure record.
FF10 and FF8: three subjects evaluated twice each record three exposures, not six — once per subject at first exposure, never per evaluation.
